title: Learning Hierarchical Patch Splitting Policies for Faster Vision Transformers
claim: Uniform patch grids waste tokens on homogeneous regions; learned adaptive splitting spends fine tokens only on semantically important content.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, same four images raw versus overlaid with patch grids
description: The figure has two panels, each a 2x2 mosaic of the same four photos: a fox in grass, a dark teal mountain range, a plate of food on a black background, and a red torii gate standing in calm water. The left panel, labeled 'Original Images', shows the clean photos. The right panel, labeled 'Split Policy Learned Image Tokenizer (Ours)', overlays thin white quadtree-style patch grids on the same photos. Grid cells are very small on the fox's face and fur, the mountain ridgeline, the food and plate, and the torii gate. They are large over the sky, water, dark background and blurry grass. The eye goes first to the fox, then to the dense grids on the subjects. Bold serif captions sit below each panel.
caption: Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization. SPLIT is an adaptive patchification framework that learns to allocate fine tokens to semantically important regions and coarse tokens to homogeneous ones, accelerating ViT inference without sacrificing accuracy.
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are bottlenecked by the length of their input token sequence. Standard patchification fixes this length with a single patch size applied across the image, regardless of regional content. Prior work on adaptive patch sizing reduces token count by assigning coarser patches to visually simple regions, but relies on noisy pixel-level heuristics such as local entropy to make patchification decisions. We argue that this compute allocation should be grounded in the model's interpretation of task relevant information, not in raw pixel statistics. We introduce Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization which learns to allocate token resolution based on what the model finds meaningful, producing shorter token sequences that are better matched to task-relevant content. SPLIT matches the accuracy of full-resolution ViT classification baselines while using 30% fewer tokens. The same gains hold on dense prediction: SPLIT achieves competitive accuracy on COCO and ADE20K, demonstrating that semantically aligned patchification generalises well beyond classification.
